abstract: Cu2O films were prepared using an improved solution immersion method, whereas ZnO/Cu2O films were prepared using an electrodeposition method. Then, the pure Cu2O film electrodes and ZnO/Cu2O film electrodes were used to reduce CO2 to CH3OH. The crystal structure, morphology, particle size, and specific surface area of pure Cu2O films prepared under different immersion times and ZnO/Cu2O films prepared under different deposition times and Zn2+ concentrations were analyzed using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and Brunauer–Emmett– Teller analysis. The electrolytic activity of the pure Cu2O film electrodes and ZnO/ Cu2O film electrodes were studied. Under the same reaction conditions, the ZnO/ Cu2O film electrode with the Zn2+ concentration of 0.05 M and the deposition time of 30 min had the highest total CH3OH yield of 315.656 μmol/cm2 and the fastest formation rate of 52.609 μmol/(cm2 h), and its faradaic efficiency was 45%, which was remarkably higher than that of pure Cu2O film electrodes under the same reaction conditions. This study highlighted that ZnO nanoparticles had a very good promotion of electrolytic CO2 reduction on Cu2O film.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
The carbon dioxide (CO2) generated by energy production and industrial transportation is the major contributor to the accumulation of CO2 in the atmosphere, which is causing the problem of global warming gradually [1]. Making use of the CO2 that has been emitted into the atmosphere is a very profound and well-researched
* Qulan Zhou qlzhou@xjtu.edu.cn
1 State Key Laboratory of Multiphase Flow in Power Engineering, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China
2 China Mobile System Integration Co., Ltd, Beijing 100052, China
1 3
technology for reducing the emission of CO2. One of the most effective methods is to use electrochemical catalytic CO2 conversion [2–8]. The essence of electrochemical catalytic conversion of CO2 is that CO2 combines with hydrogen ions to form hydrocarbons after it gains electrons at the electrode [9]. Among various products of CO2 reduction, methanol (CH3OH) is worth studying because it is liquid under normal conditions and can be easily stored and transported [10, 11]. Frese and colleagues [12, 13] first showed in the 1980s that the use of ruthenium-based and molybdenum-based electrodes could make CH3OH the main CO2 reduction product, despite a current density as low as 1 mA/cm2. During the research, copper (Cu) as well as its oxides were found to be the preferred materials for CH3OH formation in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. This was because many metal oxides of Group 4 to Group 10 metals exhibited a very low reduction rate during the CO2 reduction process, and during the reaction, hydrogen was mainly produced and the reduction of CO2 was inhibited [14–16], but the Cu species in Cu, CuO and Cu2O directly reduced CO2 to CH3OH through electron capture [17–20].
ZnO is generally used as a carrier in industrial electrolysis reactions, it has high optical transmittance and low electrical resistivity. Kannan et  al. [21] synthesized a ZnO-Fe-MXene nanocomposite and carried out a variety of characterization and electrochemical tests on them. They found that the Mxene layer could improve the electron–proton coupling transport performance of the material. Adding ZnO to the Cu2O electrode may improve the yields of CH3OH and the catalytic activity and stability of the electrode surface. Current studies on photocatalysis have proven that ZnO significantly improved the catalytic capacity of Cu2O [22–28]. In terms of electrocatalysis research, Albo et al. [29] prepared Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO electrodes by airbrushing the metal particles onto a porous carbon paper and investigated their performance of electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. The results demonstrated the good stability of Cu2O/ZnO at the stage of electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. Munir et al. [30] reported the high formation of C1–C3 products at electrodeposited Cu–Cu2O, Cu–ZnO, and Cu–Cu2O–ZnO electrodes. They suggested that C–C coupling was more inclined to Cu(0) sites than to Cu(I), and the CH3OH formation occurred through O coordination. Zhu et al. [31] constructed a ZnO@Cu2O catalyst with a core–shell structure. The experimental results showed that in the process of electrocatalytic reduction of CO2, due to the core–shell synergetic effects, the coordinating electron selectivity of the catalyst was improved, and the electron transfer was effectively accelerated, leading to its high selectivity for C2 products.
Inspired by the above research works, the aim of this work was to explore a simpler method to prepare Cu2O/ZnO electrodes and control the preparation conditions so that the prepared electrode had good surface performance and electrocatalytic ability. In addition, this work further explored the mechanism of electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CH3OH on a Cu2O/ZnO composite electrode through experiments and various characterizations.
In this work, Cu2O films were prepared using the improved solution immersion method, then ZnO was deposited on Cu2O films using an electrodeposition method. The crystal structure, morphology, particle size, and specific surface area of the films were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) analysis. Then, the pure Cu2O films
1 3
and ZnO/Cu2O films were used as electrodes for electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CH3OH. The effect of electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 under different electrode preparation times and different concentrations of Zn2+ was studied and the best preparation conditions of Cu2O films and ZnO films were obtained. Finally, a possible mechanism for efficient electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 by Cu2O films attached with ZnO was proposed.

sections.heading: Preparation of  Cu2O film electrodes
sections.text: Cu2O film electrodes were prepared using an improved solution immersion method. Copper foils (99.5%, Aladdin, China) were put into boiling saturated copper(II) sulfate (CuSO4) solution to form Cu2O. First, the copper foils (10  cm × 5  cm) were pretreated by successive immersion in 10 V% hydrochloric acid (HCl) (36.5–38.0%, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and anhydrous ethanol (AR, Aladdin) for 5–10 min to remove impurities and organic matter on the surface of the foils, and then cleaned with distilled water. After that, the pretreated copper foils were put into a saturated solution of CuSO4 at 80  °C for 1 h, 2 h, and 4 h. Then, the copper foils were placed in hot water at 80 °C for 2 h, and the water was changed several times to remove the CuSO4 on the surface of the copper foils. Finally, the copper foils were placed in a vacuum drying oven at 150  °C for 2 h, then a batch of copper foils attached with Cu2O film was obtained. The prepared samples were named Cu-1h, Cu-2h, and Cu-4h. The electrode area of all electrodes was 8  cm2. Because the acidity of the saturated CuSO4 solution increased more slowly with the extension of immersion time (as shown in Fig. S1), compared with the Cu2O film prepared by Fernando et al. [32] using a dilute solution of CuSO4, the Cu2O layer prepared in this work was thicker, the Cu2O particles were more compact and uniform, so they had better surface performance.

sections.heading: Preparation of ZnO/Cu2O film electrodes
sections.text:
Taking Zn(NO3)2 solution as the electrolyte, the cathode electrodeposition method was used to attach ZnO to Cu2O film electrodes. First, five Cu2O film electrodes with an immersion time of 2  h (Cu-2h) were selected and numbered 1–5. A certain amount of Zn(NO3)2·6H2O (99.99%, Aladdin) was dissolved in deionized water to obtain Zn(NO3)2 solutions with different concentrations of 0.02, 0.05, and 0.1 mol/L, which were used to represent low, medium, and high concentrations of Zn2+. An electrochemical workstation (CHI 760E, ShanghaiChenhua Instrument Co., Ltd., China) with a standard three-electrode system was used in all electrochemical experiments. No. 1–3 Cu2O film electrodes were electrodeposited for different deposition times (15, 30, and 45 min), using high purity graphite rod as the counter electrode and Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode. The reaction temperature
was set to 70 °C, the concentration of Zn2+ was 0.05 M, and the deposition potential was –1.2 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). No. 4 and No. 5 Cu2O film electrodes were electrodeposited with different Zn2+ concentrations (0.02 and 0.1 M), the deposition time was 30 min, and other conditions were the same as before. The prepared samples were named Zn0.05@Cu-15, Zn0.05@Cu-30, Zn0.05@Cu-45, Zn0.02@Cu-30, and Zn0.1@Cu-30. The electrode area of all electrodes was 8  cm2. Electrode preparation diagrams are shown in Figs. S2 and S3. The preparation results of all film electrodes are listed in Table 1.

sections.heading: Characterization method of film electrodes
sections.text:
The structure and morphology of the electrodes were characterized using XRD, SEM, and BET analyses. XRD patterns of all samples were collected using an X’pert Pro X-ray diffractometer (PANalytical B.V. Netherlands) in the scan range 10–80° with a speed of 5°/min, Cu Kα radiation. SEM was carried out with an SU3500 instrument (Tianmei Instrument Co., Ltd. China). The BET specific surface area and pore size of the samples were calculated from N2 adsorption isotherms at 77 K using a JW-BK132F surface area and porosity analyzer (JWGB SCI&TECH. China).
Experimental method for the electrocatalytic reduction of  CO2 to  CH3OH
The electrolyte was a saturated solution (1.14 M, 20 °C) made by dissolving sodium bicarbonate powder (GR, Aladdin) in distilled water. The two homemade glass reaction kettles were aligned according to the positions of the side openings. A proton exchange membrane (N117, Dupont, USA) was placed between two silica gel gaskets, the gaskets were clamped between the two side openings with special clamps, and then screwed down with bolts. Appropriate amounts of distilled water and electrolyte were added to the two kettles. The prepared samples were used as the working electrode, whereas a Pt wire electrode was used as the counter electrode, and a Ag/AgCl electrode (+ 0.197 V vs. SHE) was selected as the reference electrode. After the reaction kettle was sealed, the CO2 (99.999%, DSG, China) was filled into
1 3
the reaction kettle at a rate of 100 mL  min−1 through the reserved vent above the cover plate of the reaction kettle. Finally, the power supply was turned on and the experiment was started. During the reaction, the temperature of the kettle was kept at room temperature (20 °C) through the circulation of cooling water. The potential range was from −  1.0 to −  1.9  V (vs. SCE) [33]. Faradaic efficiencies were calculated based on the situation, in which six electrons were required to generate a CH3OH molecule. The products of the reaction were analyzed using a gas chromatograph (GC7890, Agilent, USA) every hour with a reaction time of 6 h. A schematic diagram of the experimental system is shown in Fig. 1.

sections.heading: Characterization
sections.text:
Fig. 2a shows the XRD patterns of the pure Cu2O films under different immersion times. Three peaks at 2θ = 36.68°, 52.63°, and 73.92° corresponded to the Cu2O diffraction planes (111), (211), and (311) (ICDD No. 01–077-0199). It could also be seen from the figure that only Cu2O was found in the prepared samples when the immersion time was 1 h and 2 h (samples: Cu-1h and Cu-2h), while CuO appeared in the Cu-4h sample when the immersion time was extended to 4h. In the figure, 2θ = 32.50°, 38.39°, 38.99°, and 58.21°correspond to the diffraction planes (110), (111), (200), and (202) of CuO (ICDD No. 00-005-0661). This may be due to the prolonged immersion in the acidic CuSO4 solution at a high temperature, resulting in the disproportionation reaction of Cu2O to generate a small amount of CuO.
Fig. 2b shows the XRD patterns of the ZnO/Cu2O films under different preparation conditions. Three peaks at 2θ = 36.57°, 52.69°, and 73.86° corresponded to the Cu2O diffraction planes (111), (211), and (311) (ICDD No. 01-077-0199). Three peaks at 2θ = 32.07°, 34.47°, and 36.53° corresponded to the ZnO diffraction planes
of (100), (002), and (101) (ICDD No. 01-089-7102). The data indicate that ZnO had successfully adhered to the surface of Cu2O.
Table 2 presents the average crystal grain size of the ZnO nanoparticles in each sample, which was calculated using the Scherer formula [34]. It can be seen that the Zn2+ concentration had a more significant effect on the formation of ZnO than the deposition time. When the Zn2+ concentration was 0.05 M and the deposition time was 30 min (sample: Zn0.05@Cu-30), the average crystal grain size of the ZnO nanoparticles was relatively moderate, 33.97 nm. When the grain size was too small, the exposed crystal faces were reduced, resulting in fewer adsorption sites for CO2, while too large a grain size led to overlap and bonding between grains, which also reduced the adsorption of CO2. Therefore, it was necessary to select the grains with moderate size.
The SEM images of pure Cu2O films under different immersion times and Cu2O films attached with ZnO under different deposition conditions are shown in Fig. 3. It can be seen from Fig. 3a–c that the size of Cu2O particles increased with the increase of immersion time, and Cu2O film with a preparation time of 2 h (sample: Cu-2h) in Fig. 3b had moderate particle size and a large covering area, which enabled more ZnO to be attached to its surface in the next step of ZnO deposition, and more active crystal faces were exposed due to the relatively moderate grain size, which retained enough CO2 adsorption sites. By comparing
1 3
the morphology characteristics of ZnO particles in Fig. 3d–h, it was found that the ZnO particles in Fig. 3d and g had smaller size and quantity, while in Fig. 3f and Fig. 3h, ZnO particles were larger and more numerous; however, too large a grain size reduced the specific surface area of particles, and these particles covered each other, and covered the whole Cu2O film, resulting in the reduction of the exposed area, which affected the adsorption and reaction of CO2 on its surface. However, the size and number of ZnO particles in Fig. 3e (sample: Zn0.05@Cu-30) were moderate with an even distribution. This result also corresponded to the previous calculation of grain size. It can also be seen from the figure that the influence of the Zn2+ concentration on the adhesion of ZnO was obviously greater than that of the deposition time. At the Zn2+ concentration of 0.02 M, although the deposition time reached 30 min, there was still very little ZnO attached to the surface of the prepared electrode.
The BET specific surface area of each sample was calculated according to the data, as shown in Fig. S4. The specific surface area of the ZnO on the sample Zn0.05@Cu-30 was the largest among all the samples, so it had a good adsorption and desorption performance.
In conclusion, the sample with 0.05 M Zn2+ concentration and 30 min deposition time (sample: Zn0.05@Cu-30) had a smaller grain size and the largest specific surface area, so it had the best surface properties.
1 3
Effect of immersion time on the electrocatalytic performance of pure Cu2O electrodes
Fig.  4 shows the change of the CH3OH formation rate with the increase in the electrochemical potential for the CO2 reduction, using pure Cu2O film electrodes under different immersion times. CH3OH formation rates of Cu-2h ranged from 0.255 to 19.188 μmol/(cm2 h), those of Cu-1h were in the range of 0.095 to 13.601 μmol/(cm2 h), and those of Cu-4h ranged from 0.160 to 18.345 μmol/ (cm2  h). The highest CH3OH production rate of Cu-2h was 4.59% higher than that of Cu-4h and 41.07% higher than that of Cu-1h. For Cu-1h, due to the short immersion time, less Cu2O was formed on the copper foil, resulting in low catalytic activity. Compared with that on the Cu-4h, Cu2O particles were smaller on the Cu-2h, which covered the surface of the copper foil more evenly. Furthermore, as can be seen from Fig.  4, the CH3OH production rate of Cu-4  h reached the maximum when the potential was about − 1.52 V (vs. SCE), and then decreased rapidly, accompanied by obvious hydrogen evolution. In contrast, the maximum CH3OH production rate of Cu-2h corresponded to a potential of −  1.63  V (vs. SCE), and it maintained a high methanol production rate over a wide potential range. The results showed that the Cu(II) species in Cu-4h led to the decrease of hydrogen overpotential, which made hydrogen evolution reaction more likely to occur on the surface of the electrode and inhibited its ability for electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. Therefore, Cu-2h had better electrocatalytic reaction performance and a higher yield of CH3OH.
1 3
Effect of ZnO addition on the electrocatalytic activity of  Cu2O electrodes
Fig. 5 shows a comparison of CH3OH formation between ZnO/Cu2O films and pure Cu2O film with the change of potential. When the potential is low (− 1.0 to − 1.2 V vs. SCE), CH3OH formation rates of all tested electrodes were similar. However, as the potential increased, the rates of CH3OH formation on the ZnO/Cu2O film electrodes were significantly higher than that of the pure Cu2O film electrodes. Among them, the CH3OH formation rate on the surface of sample Zn0.05@Cu-30 was as high as 52.609 μmol/(cm2 h). In addition, the ZnO/Cu2O film electrodes had relatively high CH3OH formation rates in a large potential range, and hydrogen evolution was not obvious. This may be because the presence of ZnO inhibited the reduction of Cu2O in the reaction process, and increased the hydrogen evolution potential of the electrodes, thus giving the electrodes better catalytic activity over a larger potential range. It can also be seen from Fig.  5 that the potentials of maximum CH3OH formation rates of ZnO/Cu2O film electrodes are slightly higher than that of pure Cu2O film electrodes (Zn0.05@Cu-15: − 1.65 V, Zn0.05@Cu-30: − 1.68 V, Zn0.05@Cu-45: − 1.70 V, Zn0.02@Cu-30: − 1.64 V and Zn0.1@Cu-30: − 1.73 V all vs. SCE). This may be because the attachment of ZnO led to the increase of the adsorption sites of CO2 on the electrodes’ surface, and facilitated the fixation of the intermediate products of CO2 reduction on the Cu(I) sites, thus reducing the reaction energy barrier. Moreover, for each electrode, the potential of maximum CH3OH formation rates increased with the increase of the attached ZnO amount.
Fig.  6 shows the relationship between CH3OH Faradaic efficiencies and potential of samples Zn0.05@Cu-30 and Cu-2h. Zn0.05@Cu-30 had the greatest Faradaic efficiency (45%) at the potential of − 1.27 V (vs. SCE), which was nearly three times the maximum Faradaic efficiency (16%, − 1.06 V vs. SCE) of Cu-2h, indicating that
CO2 reduction on the surface of Zn0.05@Cu-30 was the main reaction, and CH3OH was the main product. Meanwhile, after detecting the generated products, most of the products on the surface of Cu-2h were CO and CH4, and a strong hydrogen evolution reaction occurred on its surface, which inhibited the reduction of CO2. This result indicated that the addition of ZnO enhanced the fixation of intermediate products on the surface of Cu2O film electrodes during the conversion of CO2 to CH3OH, and effectively inhibited hydrogen evolution.
Table 3 compares the maximum faradaic efficiency for CH3OH at electrodes in this work with previous results reported in recent literature.
The performance of the pure Cu2O electrode and ZnO/Cu2O electrode in this work was comparable to or even slightly better than that of previously reported Cubased, Cu oxide, and ZnO/Cu2O materials. This may be because the Cu2O films
1 3
obtained in this work were more uniform and exposed more active crystal faces, which enabled them to adsorb CO2 effectively and fix the intermediate products in the process of CO2 conversion to CH3OH. The ZnO nanoparticles deposited under the appropriate conditions had better surface properties, which played a great role in the adsorption and transformation of CO2 on the electrode surface. The synergistic effect of ZnO and Cu2O effectively promoted the reduction of CO2 to CH3OH.
Effect of different deposition conditions on the electrocatalytic activity of  Cu2O electrodes
Fig.  7 shows the relationship of CH3OH yield on each electrode with the time obtained from the experiment at the potential of the maximum CH3OH formation rate of each electrode. By comparing the CH3OH formation on each ZnO/Cu2O electrode, it can be seen that the yield of CH3OH produced on Zn0.02@Cu-30 was the least. This was because the surface of the electrode had too little ZnO attached, and most of the Cu2O was exposed and gradually reduced in the reaction process, thus reducing the sites available for CO2 adsorption and reaction. However, for Zn0.05@ Cu-45 and Zn0.1@Cu-30, due to higher concentrations of Zn2+ or longer deposition time, excessive adhesion of ZnO on the electrodes’ surface and large grain size resulted in a significant decrease in surface porosity, which made CO2 unable to contact Cu2O directly and reduced catalytic activity. It can also be seen that with the increase of reaction time, the rate of CH3OH formation on each electrode surface gradually decreased. After gas-phase detection, it was found that the production of CH4 was gradually increased. Because CH4 was the main reduction product on the
1 3
copper electrode, it indicated that Cu2O was gradually reduced in the reaction process. Among all the samples, the CH3OH formation rate of Zn0.5@Cu-30 decreased the slowest, which also indicated that the appropriate grain size and amount of ZnO had a strong stabilization effect on Cu(I) [38].
Possible mechanism of ZnO promoting CO2 reduction on  Cu2O electrodes
It is generally believed that Cu(I) sites can effectively improve the catalytic activity and the selectivity of CO2 to CH3OH [39–41]. In addition, researchers also found that Cu(I) sites could effectively immobilize intermediate products such as carbonates ( CO2−
3 ), formate (HCOO––), and methoxy adsorbates (H3CO––) on the catalyst
surface [40]. Oxidation studies on single crystal Cu(I) show that the H3CO adsorbed on the (111) surfaces of Cu2O makes the coordinately unsaturated oxygen anions act as hydrogen abstraction sites for dehydrogenation [42]. In this case, the unsaturated oxide atoms on the (111) surfaces of cuprous oxide thin film may act as hydrogen acceptors in the reduction reaction [33]. Therefore, the amount of Cu(I) theoretically controls the reduction activity of CO2 to CH3OH. At the same time, the unsaturated oxygen ions of ZnO will also have a strong effect of adsorbing protons; in the subsequent reduction reaction, it can also provide protons in the process of H3CO conversion to CH3OH. In addition, the excellent surface properties of ZnO can effectively promote the adsorption and conversion of CO2 on the electrode surface.
Based on the above results, a possible reaction mechanism was: (a) CO2 was first adsorbed on the surface of Cu2O and ZnO (as shown in Fig. 8a), and then some CO2 adsorbed on the surface ZnO transferred to the surface of Cu2O through the pores of ZnO; (b) the CO2 was reduced to the intermediate product H3CO on the surface of Cu2O, and the oxygen atoms of ZnO and Cu2O were protonated; (c) the protons on the oxygen atoms of Cu2O and ZnO transferred to the oxygen atom of H3CO to generate CH3OH; (d) CH3OH desorbed from the surface of Cu2O, as shown in
1 3
Fig.  8d. According to the above results, the size of ZnO grains and the pore size of grains directly affected the CO2 transfer in (a), whereas the preparation time of Cu2O affected the number of Cu(I) sites, which directly affected the selectivity of the intermediates generated by CO2 and the adsorption of the intermediates on the electrode surface in (b).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
Cu2O film electrodes were prepared using an improved solution immersion method, and ZnO nanoparticles were attached to Cu2O film electrodes using an electrodeposition method. All the electrodes were characterized and used for electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. The pure Cu2O film electrode obtained by immersing and reacting in saturated CuSO4 solution for 2 h had a more uniform particle distribution, and its CH3OH yield was the highest in the pure Cu2O film electrodes, indicating that Cu(I) species may have a good selectivity to CH3OH in CO2 reduction, and significantly improved the electrode activity. In contrast, the Cu(II) sites were more prone to hydrogen evolution, which inhibited the reduction of CO2. The ZnO/Cu2O film electrode prepared under the condition of a Zn2+ concentration of 0.05 M and with the deposition time of 30 min had a very high CH3OH formation rate of 52.609 μmol/ (cm2 h), and the Faradaic efficiency reached 45%, both of which were significantly higher than other electrodes. The experimental results indicated that the appropriate Zn2+ concentration and deposition time produced ZnO with uniform shape, distribution, and large specific surface area, thereby enhancing the CO2 adsorption capacity of electrodes. Moreover, the addition of ZnO helped the intermediate products of CO2 reduction to be better fixed on Cu2O. The fundamental reaction mechanisms of CO2 reduction to form CH3OH on the surface of pure Cu2O and ZnO/Cu2O films were also elucidated, which included the transfer of CO2, reduction of CO2 to intermediate product, and proton transfer to H3CO to form CH3OH. The results of this paper provided a relatively reasonable explanation for the electrocatalytic reduction performance of pure Cu2O and ZnO/Cu2O films, and provided some new schemes for the preparation of electrodes for electrocatalytic reduction of CO2.
